The core tension lies between GSE’s operational need for signal ingestion and GSI’s validation protocol. Signals must pass through a license compliance filter (L, W, R) before being considered for adoption. If the 47-signal registry is missing (R=false), then all signals marked as 'not in registry' become unverifiable and thus queued. This introduces a dual-phase dynamic: first, a licensing gate blocks adoption unless L is open-source or explicitly allowed; second, a registry gap forces all such signals into a verification queue. Stored parts aggregation (P, A) acts as a downstream constraint, requiring new signals to be written into P before A can consume them. This creates a feedback loop where registry gaps delay signal integration, and license restrictions prevent reuse of otherwise useful components. Failure modes include: 1) unverified signals causing downstream errors, 2) license conflicts blocking adoption even when signals are valid, 3) missing registry entries preventing any signal from entering the system.
